faq.q: What kinds of product photos can I make?
faq.a: White background shots, lifestyle scenes, on-model photos, new backgrounds, feed ad images, and close-ups such as color variants or what's in the box. Each one starts from a photo of your product.

faq.q: What kind of photo should I upload?
faq.a: Use a sharp photo where the whole product is visible and nothing is cut off at the edges. Even light and a plain background help, but a clear phone photo works too.

faq.q: Which product photo type should I make first?
faq.a: Start with a clean product view for the listing. Add a lifestyle, detail, on-model, or feed image when shoppers need context or a closer look.

faq.q: Can I put a price or sale text on the photo?
faq.a: Add text after you download. Canva works well for prices, discount codes, and headlines. AI-generated lettering can contain typos, so typing it yourself keeps it accurate.

overview.h2: Pick the photo by the question it answers
overview.d: Use a white-background image when the item itself must read first. Choose a lifestyle scene when context matters, an on-model image when proportion or wear matters, a changed background when the product shot is good but the setting is wrong, and a social ad still when you need a visual with deliberate room for a headline.

overview.h2: Build a small set from one source
overview.d: A useful product gallery often starts with one clear primary view, then adds a contextual scene and a detail or worn view. Reusing the source photo lets you test those roles separately while keeping the product recognizable across the set.

input_guide.h2: Match the source photo to the output

items.d: Show the full product straight on with its important face visible; this gives a white-background result a clear shape to preserve.

items.t: For a room or table scene
items.d: Leave the whole item in frame and avoid props touching its edges, especially for mugs, candles, and small home goods.
Photograph clothing or accessories flat, on a hanger, or on a mannequin with straps, openings, and hardware visible.
Use a near view when the selling point is stitching, finish, a bottle cap, or a printed surface; do not ask a distant image to invent that detail.
Keep packaging and neighboring products out of the source frame so the resulting composition has one obvious subject.

results.h2: The output is simple to budget

items.d: Each image generation uses 24 credits. You see that cost before confirming the job.
The photo hub links to white background, lifestyle, model, background replacement, and social ad still processes.
The uploaded source and generated image stay in your account rather than being shown in a public gallery.
Download the image, then add exact prices, dates, offers, or other text in the editor where you can check every character.

scene_recipes.h2: Five ways to turn one item into a set

items.d: Make a plain first view, a breakfast table with an open book, and a close crop that keeps the handle and glaze visible.
Start with the bag laid flat, then request a shoulder-worn street scene and a quiet entryway hook shot showing the strap length.
Use a clean front view for the catalog, a marble vanity for context, and a soft-color backdrop that keeps the bottle silhouette readable.
Show the bottle upright on a white field, on a desk beside a notebook, and outdoors beside a trail, keeping the lid closed in each view.
Use a folded product shot for the listing, a sofa scene for scale, and a close-up that shows the weave without covering the edge.

good.d: Stores adding several views for the same item without arranging a new location each time.
Teams that need a new room, color, or social setting while keeping the product source unchanged.
Mugs, bottles, bags, boxes, shoes, and other items that are fully visible in the starting shot.

not_ideal.d: A source image cannot reliably supply a logo, measurement, ingredient, or texture that it never shows.
Generated scenes add context; use real measurements and product information for sizing or technical claims.

items.d: Add sale language, prices, dates, and codes yourself so the published text is exact.
Check color, count, shape, and printed details against the item you actually ship.
Use the cleanest view first, then follow with the scene or detail that answers the next shopper question.
